3-1-1.title: Types of psychological tests
3-1-1.explanation: Psychological tests are standardized procedures for administering, scoring and interpreting tasks or responses to measure personal attributes or predict outcomes. The uploaded PowerWithin material distinguishes tests from broader assessment: assessment can combine interviews, observations and tests, while a psychological test is one component of that process. Tests use specified administration and scoring procedures; They measure attributes, traits, abilities or other psychological characteristics; Assessment is broader than testing; Psychometric quality is part of test evaluation; SOURCE BASIS; PowerWithin Psychology — Unit 3 Psychological Testing; Baron & Misra and Ciccarelli & White on assessment methods. 3-3-2.title: Reliability
3-3-2.explanation: consistency or dependability of measurement test-retest; internal consistency; inter-rater; split-half. A key distinction is that Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.

inline_nudges.label: Exam caution
inline_nudges.text: Reliability is necessary but not sufficient for validity.

3-3-2.source_notes: Kaplan distinguishes reliability from validity and highlights test–retest, equivalent-form and split-half reliability. The exam decision is whether scores are consistent, not whether the test measures the intended construct. Simply Psychology describes reliability as consistency and gives test–retest and inter-observer reliability as examples. Consistency should not be confused with accuracy.

3-4-1.title: Intelligence tests
3-4-1.explanation: Intelligence tests are designed to assess cognitive abilities. The uploaded sources trace a major historical development from Binet and Simon's 1905 Binet–Simon Scale to Terman's 1916 Stanford–Binet adaptation. The sources also discuss Wechsler scales and the distinction between fluid and crystallized intelligence.
